food.text: In the early 20th century, the Revolution caused a rapid decline of Russia's elite cuisine. The new egalitarian state ideology and the disappearance of the old Imperial elites who had eaten it both drove this. A distinct Soviet cuisine was born, stressing a fusion of the Union's national cuisines, a scientific approach to diet and an industrial approach to preparing and serving food.

In 2022, shortly after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, UNESCO put the "Culture of Ukrainian borscht cooking" on its List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in Need of Urgent Safeguarding. UNESCO noted that several other countries in the region also cook borscht, and that the inscription does not imply exclusive ownership of the dish by any one country.

Ukraine, known as the "breadbasket of Europe", was among the world's top 10 agricultural exporting countries in 2020 for wheat, sugar beet, rapeseed, cucumber, rye, barley and walnuts. About 60% of its farmland is chornozem, a fertile humus-rich "black earth" soil.

The borscht recipe made with tomato paste, now standard in many Ukrainian households, replaced beetroot kvas as the dish's base ingredient only since the 1970s. Before that, the dish had traditionally been made with fermented beetroot kvas.

Vietnamese businessman Phạm Nhật Vượng established the instant noodle brand Mivina in Kharkiv in 1995. It became so popular that eventually all instant noodles in Ukraine came to be known by its brand name.

Chebureki, deep-fried turnovers filled with minced meat and onions, are a national dish of Crimean Tatar cuisine. They became widespread in Eastern Europe in the 20th century. Today they are a popular street snack in Ukraine, Russia, Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia.

Koryo-saram cuisine, from the ethnic Koreans of the former Soviet Union, is popular throughout the former Soviet Union, and dishes like morkovcha are widely sold in grocery stores. Yet it is virtually unknown in South Korea, which reportedly surprises some visitors from Russia.

The Russo-Ukrainian War has hit Ukrainian farming hard. As of May 2024, about 30% of the agricultural sector's total potential had been destroyed, and almost 20% of agricultural land was occupied as a direct result of Russia's war. Even so, by 2024 Ukraine's agricultural exports had recovered to pre-war levels.

In 2010 Nestlé bought the company that produced Mivina noodles, and also acquired the Ukrainian food producers Svitoch and Torchyn. After the Russian invasion of Ukraine, Mivina's production facilities had to be moved to Volyn Oblast. The noodles also appeared in Germany, France and Great Britain under the brand Maggi.

Ukraine's parliament lifted a ban on selling farmland in March 2020, partly under pressure from the IMF, which would only provide funding if agriculture was reformed. The land market was fully opened for the first time since independence on 1 July 2021, with conditions such as a maximum size of 100 hectares.

Lithuania's cold beet soup is an exceptionally popular summer dish today. Since 2023, its capital Vilnius has held an annual festival, the Vilnius Pink Soup Fest, to celebrate the soup's cultural heritage.

Among Crimean Tatars, chebureki is called Şırbörek or Çiborek. From old-Turkic, börek means pastry, and the Şır- part imitates the sizzling sound made when the pastry is fried. In modern Turkish the name became çiğ börek, based on a false link to çiğ, meaning "raw", though the dish is cooked.

art.text: After the Russian Revolution of 1917, officially approved art in the Soviet Union had to follow the doctrine of socialist realism. The revolution brought an artistic and cultural shift across Russia and the wider Soviet Union.

In Russia, Kasimir Malevich developed Suprematism, creating non-representational work, notably a black canvas. Alongside him, the Jack of Diamonds group with Mikhail Larionov was expressionist in nature.

After the heavy destruction of the Second World War, a project to rebuild central Kyiv turned Khreshchatyk avenue into one of the finest examples of Stalinism in architecture. It was a Soviet-era reconstruction that reshaped the heart of the Ukrainian capital.

In the 20th century, Ukrainian sculpture was deeply affected by Soviet cultural policy, war, political repression and emigration. Since 1991 it has become more integrated into international artistic networks and has paid renewed attention to public space and historical memory.

In spring 1932 the Central Committee of the Communist Party decreed that all existing literary and artistic groups be disbanded and replaced with unified associations of creative professions. The Moscow and Leningrad Union of Artists was established in August 1932, closing the history of post-revolutionary art.

Mykhailo Dzyndra left Ukraine in 1944 and lived in Germany and the United States, developing an abstract sculptural style that broke with academic canons. In the 1990s he brought more than 800 of his sculptures back to Ukraine, installing them in a self-built Museum of Modern Sculpture near Lviv.

The 1957 first All-Union Congress of Soviet Artists in Moscow established the USSR Union of Artists, uniting over 13000 professional artists. Experimentation broadened afterwards, and young scientists, workers, engineers and physicians became the most popular heroes of paintings.

The 1944 competition to redesign Khreshchatyk produced 22 individual projects, none of which was realised because of extensive critique. In 1948 the Kyiv Proekt institute submitted a final version, headed by A. Vlasov and from 1949 by Anatoly Dobrovolsky, who then dominated major capital projects for two decades.

After the 1917 revolution, the former Imperial Porcelain Factory was renamed the State Porcelain Manufactory and used for propaganda purposes. Its porcelain was meant more for decoration than everyday use, and it was exhibited outside the Soviet Union as early as the 1920s.

The 2001 reconstruction of Maidan Nezalezhnosti in Kyiv was based on Moscow's Manezhnaya Square and added an underground shopping mall and monuments, including the Independence Monument. It was criticized for pseudohistoric architecture, a smaller public space and the removal of the square's fountain.

war.text: The Russian Civil War lasted from 1917 to 1922 and was sparked by the overthrow of the Russian Provisional Government in the October Revolution. Many factions fought to decide Russia's political future, and an estimated 7 to 12 million people became casualties, mostly civilians. The Bolshevik victory led to the creation of the Russian Socialist Federative Soviet Republic and later the Soviet Union, but anti-Bolshevik resistance continued in places until 1934.

On 24 February 2022, Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the largest conflict in Europe since World War II. Russia's plan involved capturing or killing Ukraine's government, setting up filtration camps for Ukrainians, and trying and executing people involved in the Revolution of Dignity. After Mariupol was hit by renewed missile attacks on 14 March, the Ukrainian government said more than 2,500 had died, and a Russian bomb destroyed an art school sheltering around 400 people. The article says Russia has repeatedly carried out deliberate and indiscriminate attacks on civilians far from the frontline.

The Russo-Ukrainian war is generally dated to 2014, when unmarked Russian troops occupied Crimea after the flight of president Viktor Yanukovych. Russia annexed Crimea in March 2014 after an illegitimate referendum held under Russian occupation. In April 2014 Russian-backed militants seized towns in the Donbas region, and the first deaths came on 13 April, when Russian paramilitaries fired on Ukrainian security officers outside Sloviansk and killed Gennady Bilichenko. On 17 April they kidnapped the local councillor Volodymyr Rybak, and his body was dumped in a river, tortured and mutilated, along with the bodies of two Maidan activists.

The Russian Civil War became a full-scale conflict in May-June 1918. Its two largest combatants were the Red Army, fighting for a Bolshevik-led socialist state under Vladimir Lenin, and the White movement, led mainly by right-leaning officers of the Russian Empire and united around Alexander Kolchak. To fill its ranks, the Red Army took rural hostages and shot them when necessary to force compliance with conscription, and sometimes held the families of former Tsarist officers hostage to ensure their loyalty. In the field, Cheka punitive detachments followed the Red Army, conducting summary executions of soldiers and officers who deserted or retreated.

Historians disagree about when the current war began. Ukrainian-American historian Serhii Plokhy declined to treat 24 February 2022 as its start, arguing that the war began eight years earlier, on 27 February 2014. Paul D'Anieri instead describes a limited war in 2014 and a much less limited war in 2022.

By April 2022, the invasion's initial goal of a rapid Russian victory via decapitation had failed. Ukraine pushed back the northern arm of the invasion and prevented the capture of Kyiv. Unable to win quickly, Russian forces switched to standoff weapons, indiscriminate bombing and siege warfare. When Ukrainian forces retook the Bucha area in early April, evidence of war crimes was uncovered there. The war then shifted to more conventional fighting in the south and east of Ukraine.

The Ukrainian War of Independence lasted from March 1917 to November 1921 and was part of the wider Russian Civil War. Its belligerents included Ukrainian nationalists, Ukrainian anarchists, German and Austro-Hungarian forces, the White Russian Volunteer Army, and Second Polish Republic forces. Most of the independent Ukrainian republic was absorbed into the Ukrainian SSR between 1919 and 1920.

In January 1918 Soviet forces under Lt. Col. Muravyov invaded Ukraine and took Kiev, where the Central Council of Ukraine held power. With the help of the Kiev Arsenal Uprising, the Bolsheviks captured the city on 26 January.

In June 1918 the Volunteer Army, numbering some 9,000 men, began its Second Kuban campaign. It captured Yekaterinodar on 16 August, followed by Armavir and Stavropol. By early 1919 it controlled the Northern Caucasus. In March 1920, the Novorossiysk evacuation left about 20,000 of Denikin's men behind, to be dispersed or captured by the Red Army.

Ethnic minorities have suffered disproportionately high casualties in the Russian military in Ukraine. In October 2022, the Russian regions with the highest death tolls were Dagestan, Tuva, and Buryatia, all minority regions. Analysts warned that this would have long-term destructive impacts on these communities.

Between 2019 and 2021, Russia issued over 650,000 internal Russian passports to Ukrainians. Over the same years, conflict-related civilian deaths in Ukraine were 27 in 2019, 26 in 2020 and 25 in 2021, over half of them from mines and unexploded ordnance.

literature.text: In the 1970s, some of the most prominent Russian authors were banned from publishing and prosecuted for anti-Soviet sentiments or for "parasitism". Writers Yuli Daniel and Leonid Borodin were imprisoned, and Solzhenitsyn and Nobel Prize-winning poet Joseph Brodsky were expelled from the country. Many others had to emigrate to the West. Kari Unksova and Yury Dombrovsky were murdered, Dombrovsky shortly after publishing his novel The Faculty of Useless Knowledge in 1975.
Banned Soviet books were not officially published until the perestroika period of the 1980s. Fans kept them alive by reprinting them manually in a practice called "samizdat", meaning self-publishing.

Russian-language literature includes writers of many ethnic origins, such as the Kyrgyz novelist Chinghiz Aitmatov. Vasil Bykaŭ wrote in Belarusian but translated his own works into Russian. The Dagestani poet Rasul Gamzatov is omitted, because he wrote primarily in a native language of Russia's indigenous groups.

The collapse of the Russian Empire and the founding of the Ukrainian People's Republic (1917–1920) sparked an explosion in Ukrainian-language publishing. According to estimates, more than 1,000 Ukrainian-language periodicals appeared in the revolutionary period, and book output in Ukrainian increased many times over.

From the late 1960s, print runs of Russian-language books in Ukraine consistently exceeded those of Ukrainian-language books, as part of an intensified Russification. Persecution of writers and dissidents resumed in the 1960s and 1970s, and the Sixtiers generation suffered arrests, internal exile and publishing bans.
Volodymyr Vladko, called the "Ukrainian Jules Verne", wrote The Roboters Are Coming in 1929. It is described as perhaps the first novel in world science fiction about robots to use a similar term.

Yury Dombrovsky (1909–1978) was murdered, shortly after publishing his novel The Faculty of Useless Knowledge in 1975. The poet Kari Unksova (1941–1983) was murdered as well. Both are listed among the Soviet nonconformist writers who were banned or prosecuted in the 1970s, and their books were not published officially until the perestroika period of the 1980s.

Venedikt Yerofeyev (1938–1990) and Oleg Grigoriev (1943–1992) are described as having "emigrated" to alcoholism, while poet Yury Aikhenvald (1928–1993), repressed still in Stalinist years, turned to translations. Other banned writers had to emigrate to the West, and Kari Unksova and Yury Dombrovsky were murdered. Their books were not published officially until the 1980s, though fans reprinted them by hand as samizdat.
Oles Berdnyk, a Soviet-era dissident, is described as the most significant classic Ukrainian science-fiction writer. Ihor Rosokhovatskyi coined the Ukrainian word for cyborg, "syhom".

The last major reform of Russian orthography was carried out in 1917–1918. The first attempt at reforming it had been made in 1708–1710. Russian is written in a Cyrillic alphabet adapted from Old Church Slavonic.

The first anthology of Ukrainian fantasy stories, Ohnenyi zmiy (The Fiery Dragon), was published in 1990. The first anthology of Ukrainian horror stories followed in 2000, and Kyiv hosted the Eurocon science fiction convention in 2006 and 2013.

science.text: In 1922, Alexander Friedmann became the first scientist to propose an expanding universe model. It greatly influenced cosmology throughout the 20th century. He was one of several Russian and Soviet scientists who ranked among the world leaders in physics.

Georgiy Gamov proposed the theory of alpha decay of a nucleus via tunnelling in 1928. He was also an author of the Big Bang theory. His work placed Soviet-era physics at the center of nuclear and cosmological thinking.

Russian cosmism blended science, religion and metaphysics into one worldview. It held that humanity had a cosmic destiny and that technology could win control over nature and open the way to space. Though suppressed in the Soviet era, it influenced Soviet space exploration.

In 1932, Dmitri Ivanenko was the first to propose the proton-neutron model of atomic nuclei. He also proposed the nuclear shell model in the same year. Both ideas shaped how physicists understand the atomic nucleus.

Konstantin Tsiolkovsky's work in astronautics and space travel laid the foundations for modern cosmonautics. He belonged to the cosmist movement, which grew amid a burst of early twentieth-century scientific investigation into interplanetary travel. That interest was largely driven by fiction writers such as Jules Verne and H. G. Wells.

Alexander Bogdanov, a Russian and later Soviet physician and Bolshevik revolutionary, explored the possibility of human rejuvenation through blood transfusion. He saw heterochronic transfusions as an alliance between generations, in which the old benefited from the young blood and the young received immunities from the elders' blood. Ironically, he died in 1928 as a result of a hemolytic transfusion reaction.
Gleb Kotelnikov invented the knapsack parachute, and Evgeniy Chertovsky introduced the pressure suit. Both were individual inventors who made important contributions to aircraft technology.

In 1957, Laika, a Soviet space dog, became the first animal to orbit the Earth aboard Sputnik 2. In 1968, Zond 5 carried two tortoises and other life forms around the Moon, making them the first Earthlings to do so.

Vladimir Vernadsky developed the notion of the noosphere. Fellow cosmist Alexander Chizhevsky pioneered heliobiology, the study of the sun's effect on biology. Both were counted among the thinkers of Russian cosmism.

In the 1990s, a crisis sharply cut state support for science and technology in Russia. Many scientists and university graduates moved to Western Europe or the United States. Support improved in the 2000s, when the government launched a modernisation and innovation campaign with mixed success.

After the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, tens of thousands of tech workers fled Russia, and many scientific agreements with Western countries ended. Russia ranked 60th in the Global Innovation Index in 2025, down from 45th in 2021.

The cosmist Alexander Chizhevsky (1897 to 1964) was a pioneer of heliobiology, the study of the sun's effect on biology. A minor planet, 3113 Chizhevskij, discovered by Nikolai Stepanovich Chernykh in 1978, is named after him.
A minor planet, 3113 Chizhevskij, honors the heliobiology pioneer Alexander Chizhevsky. It was discovered in 1978 by Soviet astronomer Nikolai Stepanovich Chernykh.

In 2015, the Russian Academy of Sciences began awarding the honorary rank of RAS Professor on a competitive basis to top researchers with Russian citizenship. As of January 2026, 797 scientists held it. Some later became corresponding members or full academicians.

In April 1942 Soviet nuclear physicist Georgy Flyorov wrote to Joseph Stalin noting the absence of articles on nuclear fission in American journals. American scientists had begun avoiding publishing military-related research, and this silence led the Soviet Union to establish its own atomic bomb project.

politics.text: Russia's entry into World War I unfolded over days in July 1914. Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia, a Russian ally, and Germany declared war on Russia on August 1, 1914. Within days, France and Britain were also drawn in.
politics.source_title: Russian entry into World War I

politics.text: In 1917, mass unrest in Petrograd and army mutinies led to the February Revolution. Nicholas II abdicated, the Provisional Government took over, and the Russian Republic was proclaimed. Later that year the Bolsheviks overthrew the republic in the October Revolution.

The Soviet Union was declared on December 30, 1922, after the Bolsheviks won the Russian Civil War. It brought together Russia, Ukraine, Belarus and Transcaucasia, with Lenin as its leader. The republics had signed a treaty of union the day before.

The abdication of Nicholas II on 15 March 1917 ended 304 years of Romanov rule. On the night of 16 July 1918, Bolsheviks took Nicholas II, Alexandra, their five children and four servants down to a cellar in the Ipatiev House and gunned them down. Those who survived the shooting were stabbed to death, and some of the children, including the young and frail Tsesarevich, would not die from multiple close-range bullet wounds or bayonet stabs, so the gunmen shot each again, and two daughters still alive 10 minutes later were bludgeoned to death with a rifle butt. Of the House of Romanov's 65 members, 47 survivors went into exile abroad.

Tsar Nicholas II ordered the mobilization of Russian forces on July 30, 1914, to deter Austria-Hungary from invading Serbia. Historian Christopher Clark calls it one of the most critical decisions of the July Crisis. It came before Germany declared a state of imminent war.
politics.source_title: Russian entry into World War I

politics.text: Russia was one of four continental European empires to collapse as a result of World War I, along with Germany, Austria-Hungary and the Ottoman Empire. The casualties were enormous: the defeat at Tannenberg destroyed the entire second army, the two defeats at the Masurian Lakes cost about 100,000 and 200,000 casualties, and the Brusilov offensive cost approximately one million men. Along with military setbacks and severe food and fuel shortages in the cities, this fed widespread discontent with the monarchy.

Ukraine lost 60% of its GDP between 1991 and 1999 after the Soviet Union dissolved. Hyperinflation peaked at 10,000% in 1993. Mass privatisation of state property created a class of extremely powerful and rich individuals known as oligarchs.

Stalin deported all Kalmyks to Siberia in 1943, and around half of the 97,000 to 98,000 deported died there before the survivors were allowed to return home in 1957. The Soviet government also forbade teaching the Kalmyk language during the deportation. Earlier, 71,000 to 72,000 Kalmyks (around half the population, possibly 93,000) had died in the Russian famine of 1921-22, after Bolshevik Russia refused Mongolia's proposal to relocate them. Under a Russian Federation law of April 26, 1991, the repressions against Kalmyks and other peoples were qualified as acts of genocide.

The Russian Civil War pitted the Bolsheviks against the Whites, a broad, ideologically diverse anti-Bolshevik coalition, and the war was marked by vicious atrocities from both sides. The Russian imperial family, including Nicholas, was executed by a mob of Bolshevik soldiers on the night of July 16-17, 1918, possibly on the orders of Lenin.

The Soviet Union adopted its emblem in 1923, and it remained in use until the dissolution in 1991. Ribbons carried inscriptions in the languages of the republics. In the final 1956 version the Finnish inscription was removed after the Karelo-Finnish SSR became the Karelian ASSR.

Under Vladimir Putin's government, the 2014 centenary of World War I tended to glorify a strong state with authoritarian and Russian nationalist connotations. Speeches stressed the continuity of Russia, which repelled Napoleon in 1812 and triumphed over Nazism in 1945. This coincided with Ukraine's revolution and the annexation of Crimea.

After the February Revolution of 1917, a decree of the Provisional Government granted all members of the imperial family the surname Romanov. The only exceptions were the morganatic descendants of Grand Duke Dmitri Pavlovich, who took the surname Ilyinsky in exile.

Russia's current coat of arms was approved by presidential Decree No. 2050 on 30 November 1993. On 25 December 2000, Vladimir Putin signed a federal constitutional law keeping the 1993 version as the state symbol. Both texts use the same drawing by artist Yevgeny Ukhnalyov.

philosophy.text: Russian cosmism was a philosophical and cultural movement that blended science, religion, and metaphysics into one worldview. It held that humanity has a cosmic destiny, could achieve immortality, and should use science and technology to master nature and explore space.

In 1921, Gustav Shpet founded the Institute of Scientific Philosophy, the ancestor of Russia's central philosophical research institution. That summer the philosophy department of the University of Moscow had been disbanded, and philosophers such as Semyon Frank and Ivan Ilyin tried to set up temporary courses at the new institute.
philosophy.source_title: Institute of Philosophy, Russian Academy of Sciences

philosophy.text: Historian M. A. Gillespie says nihilism was at the core of revolutionary thought in Russia in the lead-up to the Russian Revolution. Professor T. J. J. Altizer goes further, saying Russian nihilism had its deepest expression in a Bolshevist nihilism of the 20th century.

In 1924 the Society of Militant Materialists was founded, renamed Militant Dialectical Materialists in 1928. It consisted predominately of Marxist philosophers (exclusively after 1928) grouped around Under the Banner of Marxism, and aimed to combat religious and idealistic views among scientists, scholars and intellectuals.

Russian cosmism was a philosophical and cultural movement that emerged in late 19th- and early 20th-century Russia, joining science, religion and metaphysics. Nikolai Fedorov advocated the abolition of death and the resurrection of ancestors through scientific means. Though suppressed in the Soviet era, it influenced Soviet space exploration.

Nikolai Fedorov, a key figure in Russian cosmism, advocated the abolition of death and the resurrection of ancestors through scientific means. Cosmism was suppressed during the Soviet era, yet it still influenced Soviet space exploration and transhumanism.

Konstantin Tsiolkovsky published the first serious scientific work on space travel in 1903. He also wrote "The Will of the Universe; Unknown Intelligent Forces", in which he set out a philosophy of panpsychism and predicted that humans would eventually colonize the Milky Way.

After being expelled from the party in 1927 and losing his citizenship in 1929, Leon Trotsky developed his own interpretation of Marxism in exile, called Trotskyism. He attacked Stalin's doctrine of Socialism in One Country, claiming it was incongruent with the ideology of the revolution.
Tsiolkovsky did not believe in traditional religious cosmology. He believed instead in a cosmic being that governed humans.

The Bolsheviks soon put a stop to the attempt to set up temporary philosophy courses, and Semyon Frank and Ivan Ilyin were among the deportees sent into exile on the philosophers' ships. Shpet's name was also put forward for deportation, but Anatoli Lunacharsky, the People's Commissar for Education, intervened and he was allowed to remain in Russia.
philosophy.source_title: Institute of Philosophy, Russian Academy of Sciences

philosophy.text: Eventually, Trotsky settled in Mexico City and founded a base of operations there for himself and his supporters. In 1937, at the height of the Great Purge, he published The Revolution Betrayed, which outlined his ideological contradictions with Stalin and argued that Stalin was guilty of subverting and debasing the 1917 revolution. He continued to vocally criticize Stalin and Stalinism until his assassination in 1940 on Stalin's orders.

Georgii Plekhanov and Vladimir Lenin, the two thinkers most responsible for developing Marxism in Russia, credited Chernyshevskii with 'massive' and 'overwhelming' influence on them respectively. During the communist period, the principal nihilist theoreticians were officially lionized as 'Russian revolutionary democrats'.

Vladimir Vernadsky (1863 to 1945) developed the notion of a noosphere, while Alexander Chizhevsky (1897 to 1964) pioneered "heliobiology", the study of the sun's effect on biology. A minor planet discovered by Soviet astronomer Nikolai Stepanovich Chernykh in 1978, 3113 Chizhevskij, is named after Chizhevsky.

In 1929 an Institute of Philosophy of the Communist Academy was created under Abram Deborin. In 1936 it was folded into the Academy of Sciences of the USSR under Vladimir Adoratsky, and since the end of 1991 the institution has belonged to the Russian Academy of Sciences.
philosophy.source_title: Institute of Philosophy, Russian Academy of Sciences

culture.text: Tea is considered the de facto national beverage of Russia, partly because of the country's cold northern climate. It is closely associated with traditional Russian culture and is drunk all day, especially at the end of meals with dessert.

Although ice hockey was only introduced during the Soviet era, the national team soon dominated internationally. Between 1954 and 1991 it won gold at seven of the nine Olympics and 19 of the 30 World Championships it contested.
Football is the most popular sport in Russia. The Soviet Union national football team became the first European champions by winning Euro 1960. Russia later hosted the 2018 FIFA World Cup.

Russians brew tea in two steps. First a strong concentrate called zavarka is made in a small teapot, then each person pours some into a cup and dilutes it with hot water. This lets everyone make their tea as strong and as hot as they like.

The samovar was widely used to boil water for tea until the middle of the 20th century. Then gas stoves spread through newly mass-constructed apartment buildings, and kettles largely replaced it. From the 1990s, electric kettles became the norm.

Valeri Kharlamov, Sergei Makarov, Viacheslav Fetisov and Vladislav Tretiak hold four of the six positions on the IIHF Team of the Century. After the breakup of the Soviet Union, Russia endured a 15-year gold medal drought, and many prominent players made their careers in the NHL.

In 1922 and 1926 the Bolshevik regime produced criminal codes that left out any article prohibiting homosexual sex, though homosexuals in Russia were still persecuted and sacked from their jobs. Under Joseph Stalin, the Soviet Union recriminalized homosexuality in a decree signed in 1933. The new Article 121 punished "muzhelozhstvo" with up to 5 years in prison and brought raids and arrests, while female homosexuals were sent to mental institutions. Homosexuality was not officially declassified as a mental illness until 1999.

In occupied Melitopol in 2022, Russian troops stole a 4th-century golden helmet dating to the Scythian kingdom, worth millions of dollars. The local museum director had hidden other Scythian gold artifacts shortly before the Russian army occupied the city. Soldiers tried to force her to reveal where it was, threatened her at gunpoint, and abducted her when she refused to cooperate. She was interrogated but was ultimately allowed to leave Russian-held territory.
culture.source_title: Art theft and looting by Russia during the invasion of Ukraine

culture.text: Using your personal teaspoon to add sugar from the shared bowl is considered impolite in Russia. Tea drinking has no formal ceremony, and it is seen as the best time for small talk. The end of the tea signals the end of the meal.
The Kontinental Hockey League (KHL) was founded in 2008 as a rival of the NHL. Russia also won back to back gold medals at the 2008 and 2009 World Championships.
